prompt: What does steganography mainly aim to hide?

options.text: The fact that a message exists at all
What the message says, by using a key
options.why: Protecting what a message says with a key is what cryptography does.

options.text: The size of the carrier file
options.why: Steganography doesn't aim to hide the carrier's size; an unexpected size can even give it away.

options.text: Who sent the message
options.why: Hiding the sender's identity is anonymity, not steganography.

explanation: Cryptography asks "What does this message say?" and protects contents. Steganography asks "Is there a message here?" and conceals that communication exists.

prompt: Steganography on its own hides that a message exists, but does not protect what the message says.
explanation: It conceals presence, not meaning. To protect both, encrypt the message and then embed the ciphertext. Neither method guarantees the carrier will avoid detection.

prompt: Why can least-significant-bit (LSB) substitution be hard to spot by eye?

options.text: Each pixel's colour changes only very slightly
It encrypts the image so the hidden part looks like noise
options.why: LSB embedding doesn't encrypt the image; it makes tiny value changes that are hard to see.

options.text: It only works on black-and-white images, which hide changes
options.why: LSB embedding works on colour images too; the changes are small, not limited to black and white.

options.text: It removes the image's metadata, which is where tools look
options.why: LSB embedding changes pixel values, not metadata, and analysis tools look at the pixels.

explanation: A tiny change per pixel is hard to see, but accumulated changes or statistical patterns can still be detected. Hard to see does not mean undetectable.

prompt: If an image looks identical to the original, it has not been altered.
explanation: Visual similarity does not prove an image is safe or unchanged. LSB changes are designed to be hard to see.

prompt: A sender encrypts a message and then hides the ciphertext inside an image. What does each step contribute?

options.text: Encryption hides the meaning; steganography hides that a message exists
Encryption hides that a message exists; steganography hides the meaning
options.why: This swaps the two: encryption protects meaning and steganography hides existence.

options.text: Both hide the meaning, so using the two together adds nothing new
options.why: They do different jobs: one hides meaning, the other hides that a message exists.

options.text: Together they guarantee no analysis tool can ever detect the image
options.why: Neither method guarantees the carrier will pass every analysis tool unnoticed.

explanation: The methods can be combined, but neither guarantees the carrier will look normal to every analysis tool.

prompt: The bit sequence 010101... has equal counts of 0s and 1s. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Balanced counts don't mean unpredictable: the pattern is easy to guess
Equal numbers of 0s and 1s show the sequence is cryptographically random
options.why: Balanced counts don't show unpredictability; this sequence is completely predictable.

options.text: A repeating pattern like this one always means data is hidden inside
options.why: A repeating pattern is just structure; it doesn't indicate hidden data.

options.text: Entropy can only be measured for text, so binary sequences don't count
options.why: Entropy can be measured for any symbols, including bits.

explanation: The result depends on which data and probability model are measured. A balanced but repeating pattern can still be predictable.

prompt: During file triage, part of a file has very high Shannon entropy. What is the most defensible conclusion?

options.text: It may be compressed, encrypted or packed, so investigate further
It proves the file contains hidden steganographic data inside it
options.why: High entropy is common in ordinary compressed or encrypted files; it doesn't prove hidden data.

options.text: It proves the file is malware, because normal files never look random
options.why: Many legitimate files look random, such as zip archives and media.

options.text: It shows the data is safe, as it must come from a secure random generator
options.why: A high entropy score says nothing about safety or where the data came from.

explanation: Ordinary media and legitimate encrypted files can also have high entropy. A score does not identify the cause or prove a file is unsafe.

prompt: You need to generate password-reset tokens. What should you use?

options.text: The platform's cryptographically secure random generator
A custom generator that scores highly on entropy tests
options.why: A good score on entropy tests doesn't make a homemade generator unpredictable to attackers.

options.text: The current time, hashed with SHA-256 to look random
options.why: Time values are guessable, and hashing a guessable input stays guessable.

options.text: `Math.random()`, seeded with the user's ID for uniqueness
options.why: `Math.random()` isn't cryptographically secure, and a user ID is a guessable seed.

explanation: A high measured entropy score does not establish cryptographic unpredictability. Do not build a security-sensitive generator yourself.

prompt: Put these steps of a steganographic exchange in order.
steps: The sender chooses a message and a carrier file
The sender embeds the message into the carrier
The carrier, now holding the message, is sent or stored
The recipient extracts the hidden message
explanation: A payload may be compressed or encrypted before embedding, and some methods use a key. These are choices, not requirements of every method.

prompt: Re-saving, resizing or converting an image may damage or remove an LSB payload.
explanation: LSB substitution is fragile: lossy re-saving, cropping or resizing changes pixel values and can destroy the hidden bits. Transform-domain methods survive compression better.

prompt: Which of these are useful things to check when looking for hidden data in a file? Select all that apply.

options.text: Unexpected changes to its size, format or metadata
Statistical patterns in its pixel or audio data that differ from normal files
Visible or audible distortion
Odd context, such as an unexpected upload, transfer or program opening it
Its file extension, since a normal extension means nothing is hidden
options.why: An extension is a user-supplied label; it can't show a file is free of hidden data.

explanation: Simple checks can miss sophisticated embedding. Comparing with a known original helps, but an original is often unavailable.

prompt: A carrier file showing signs of hidden data is a lead to investigate rather than proof of malicious intent.
explanation: Steganography has legitimate uses such as watermarking and protecting people at risk. A suspicious carrier is an investigation lead.

prompt: In the path `invoice.pdf:Zone.Identifier`, what does the colon introduce?

options.text: A named stream attached to the same file, not a separate file
A second, separate file stored in the same folder
options.why: The stream belongs to invoice.pdf itself; no separate file is created.

options.text: A drive letter, as at the start of a Windows path
options.why: Drive letters come at the start of a path, before the folder names, not after a filename.

options.text: A permission flag that controls who can open it
options.why: NTFS permissions are stored separately; the colon names a stream.

explanation: The colon introduces a stream name. It does not create a second, ordinary file.

prompt: What does Windows typically use the `Zone.Identifier` stream for?

options.text: Recording download-origin information
Storing the file's encryption key
options.why: Encryption keys aren't stored in Zone.Identifier; it records where a file came from.

options.text: Holding a backup of the file
options.why: It doesn't hold a backup; it's a small note about origin.

options.text: Logging every program that opened the file
options.why: It doesn't log program access; it marks download origin.

explanation: It can record that a file came from an Internet zone. Its presence alone is not suspicious.

prompt: An alternate data stream runs its contents automatically when the file is opened.
explanation: A named stream does not execute itself. Another program or action must read or execute its content.

prompt: Which statements about NTFS alternate data streams are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tools can list a file's streams so each one can be inspected
A named stream's presence alone shows the file is malicious
options.why: Windows itself creates named streams, for example to mark downloaded files, so presence alone proves nothing.

options.text: FAT32 and exFAT also support named streams
options.why: Named streams are an NTFS feature; FAT32 and exFAT don't support them.

explanation: Only NTFS supports named streams among the three. Enumerate streams explicitly when you need the complete file object.

prompt: Steganography or alternate data stream? Match each statement.

pairs.item: Hides data inside the content of a carrier, such as an image's pixels
pairs.why: Steganography hides data inside the carrier itself.

pairs.item: Attaches an extra named stream to a file on NTFS
pairs.why: Named streams are an NTFS feature attached to a file.

pairs.item: Found by listing all the streams attached to a file
pairs.why: Streams show up when you list them; steganography doesn't.

pairs.item: Looked for through statistical patterns and visible or audible distortion
pairs.why: Steganalysis looks for statistical and visual traces.
Watermarking hides marks inside the content.

pairs.item: Legitimate use: recording that a file came from an Internet zone
pairs.why: Windows records download origin in a named stream.

explanation: Steganography changes a carrier's representation; ADS adds a named stream to a file. The defensive questions differ accordingly.

prompt: What is the term for analysis that looks for evidence a carrier file contains hidden data?
explanation: Steganalysis combines file properties, statistical patterns, artefacts and context. One signal is rarely enough to prove intent.

prompt: An upload scanner reads only the default stream of files on an NTFS volume. What risk does this create?

options.text: Content hidden in other named streams could be missed
The scanner will run too slowly on large NTFS volumes
options.why: The risk isn't speed; content in other named streams is never inspected.

options.text: The scanner will flag every NTFS file as malicious by mistake
options.why: Reading only the default stream would miss things, not flag every file.

options.text: None, because an NTFS file only ever has one stream
options.why: NTFS files can have several named streams alongside the default one.

explanation: Know which file content your application, scanner and storage tools actually inspect, and apply checks to the whole file object.

prompt: Match each byte pattern to its Shannon entropy.

pairs.item: Every byte has the same value
pairs.why: The next value is always known, so there is no uncertainty.
A fair binary outcome carries one bit of uncertainty.
This is the maximum for one byte.

explanation: Shannon entropy is the average information, in bits, per outcome. For bytes it runs from 0 to 8, but a frequency count alone can miss order: a balanced, repeating pattern is still predictable.

prompt: Is each use of steganography legitimate or abuse?

pairs.item: Covert communication for people at risk

explanation: The same technique serves protective and harmful purposes, so a suspicious carrier is a lead to investigate, not proof of malicious intent.
